passage:
Class 5 note, Thursday. Imran, class teacher.
During our lesson on families, Bidisha put her hand up and asked, 'Why do grown-ups say "Respect your elders" every time they're losing an argument?' A few children laughed. She went red but didn't take the question back. After class she told me her Ma says it whenever she asks why she can't go to the park with friends. I explained that respect means being polite and caring, like not shouting and helping an elder carry things, not being scared or never asking questions. She asked if she could still say 'I don't agree' nicely. I said yes, and we practised it once. I will mention our talk to her Ma at the parent meeting.

qa.q: What did Bidisha practise with Imran?
How did Bidisha feel when a few children laughed at her question?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, going red, but also determined, since she didn't take the question back.

qa.q: What did Imran's explanation give Bidisha?
qa.a: A clear meaning of respect as courtesy and care rather than fear, plus a polite way to disagree, so she can keep her manners and her voice.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's Ma see things after hearing about this at the parent meeting?
qa.a: Her Ma might realise that 'respect your elders' leaves Bidisha feeling shut down, and try giving real reasons about the park instead.

grounding: Illustrates a child who is told to respect elders whenever adults disagree, and a teacher who explains respect as courtesy and care rather than fear.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Dadi switched off my cartoon halfway because it was time for her serial, even though I asked first. When I said that wasn't fair, Papa said, 'Respect your elders, Aparna,' and that was the end of it. Why? Being older doesn't make you right about the TV! I went to my room and cried into the pillow so nobody would hear.
Later Madhav Bhaiya came in. He said respect isn't being scared of Dadi, it's being kind to her, like when I oil her hair on Sundays. He said I can still tell her 'I asked first' in a nice voice. Tomorrow I'll try. Maybe we can take turns.
Aparna, age 10

qa.q: What does Aparna do for Dadi on Sundays?
qa.a: Aparna oils Dadi's hair on Sundays.

qa.q: Why did Aparna cry into the pillow, and what was Aparna feeling?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and unheard, because Papa ended the argument with 'respect your elders' instead of a reason.

qa.q: How did Madhav Bhaiya's explanation help Aparna?
qa.a: It showed respect as kindness rather than fear and gave Aparna a polite way to speak up, so Aparna can keep good manners and still have a voice.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel if Aparna says 'I asked first' nicely and offers to take turns?
qa.a: Dadi may feel respected rather than challenged, and could be glad to share the TV.

grounding: Shows a child told to respect elders without any reason when adults disagree, and an older sibling explaining respect as care, not fear, so the child keeps both manners and a voice.
